# Best Cardio Machine for Gamers: How Games and Leaderboards Make Workouts More Engaging


Opponents top left, live split and stroke rate along the bottom. The workout is the input.


**Cardio gets abandoned because it gets boring, not because it gets hard.** Gamified fitness fixes that by giving a workout something to aim at other than the clock: a score to beat, a challenge to finish, a player to catch, a personal best to move. When the session has a goal inside it, the minutes stop being the thing you are counting.


This is a guide to why that works, who it works for, and what to look for in an interactive cardio machine. Aviron shows up as the example because it is what we build, but the principles apply whatever you end up buying.


## In this article

## Why Cardio Is Hard to Stick With


Almost nobody quits cardio because it is too difficult. People quit because it is the same.


A treadmill, a rower and a bike all ask you to repeat one movement, and the feedback you get in return is a handful of numbers: time elapsed, distance covered, calories burned. Those numbers describe the workout, but none of them give you anything to chase while you are in it. The only real goal is finishing.


That is a thin thing to hold your attention for half an hour, and it gets thinner with repetition. By week three, the session has no shape beyond its own length, and the thought running through your head is some version of *I have 25 minutes left* . Motivation tends to fall away not at the hard moments but at the boring ones.


It is worth saying plainly that this is not a character flaw. Equipment that gives you nothing to engage with is competing for your attention against a phone designed by people who are very good at holding it. Losing that contest is the expected outcome, not a personal failing.


## What Is Gamified Fitness?


**Gamified fitness takes the things that make games compelling and applies them to exercise.** Points, scores, levels, challenges, achievements, progress bars, competition and leaderboards are all mechanisms for making effort feel purposeful, and none of them are specific to video games.


In practice it means a workout is structured like a game rather than like a timer. You might be collecting something, defending something, racing someone, working through stages, or trying to hold a target to keep a streak alive. The physical work is identical. What changes is what you are paying attention to while you do it.


There is a useful distinction hiding here, and it separates the good implementations from the marketing. In genuine gamified fitness, **your effort is the input** . Pull harder and the thing on screen responds. Ease off and you lose ground. In the weaker version, a game or a video simply plays near you while you exercise independently of it, and the two never actually meet.


## Why Games Make Cardio More Engaging


The difference shows up in what you are thinking about.


In a conventional session, attention turns inward. You notice your breathing, your legs, the ache building, and the clock. Every one of those signals is telling you how much is left to endure.


In a game-based session, attention has somewhere else to go. You are trying to beat a score, finish a challenge, catch the player ahead of you, or better the split you set last Tuesday. The effort has not changed, but you are no longer monitoring it, and a workout you are not monitoring tends to feel shorter and easier than one you are.


That is not a trick of marketing, it is a reasonably well studied effect. Directing attention away from fatigue signals measurably lowers how hard a given workload feels, and how a session feels while it is happening turns out to be a better predictor of whether you do it again than how you feel afterwards. We went through the research in[why exercise feels easier when it is actually enjoyable](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/why-exercise-feels-easier-when-enjoyable) .


The practical version is simpler. A workout with a goal inside it gives you a reason to start tomorrow. A workout with only a duration gives you a reason to skip.


## Why Leaderboards Appeal to Competitive People


Of all the game mechanics that transfer to exercise, leaderboards do the most work, because they add something a solo workout cannot: someone else who might beat you.


That creates a kind of accountability that does not rely on discipline. You are not talking yourself into a session, you are trying not to lose a position. One Aviron member put it directly:


"I am super competitive... and having leaderboards with Aviron helps keep me motivated to get extra cardio in."


Verified Aviron buyer


Note what is actually being described there. Not motivation to complete the workout that was already planned, but motivation to do **extra** cardio. That is a meaningful difference. The leaderboard is not helping them finish, it is making them want more.


Leaderboards also work in a quieter way that is easy to overlook. They give you a benchmark. Even if you never overtake anyone, seeing where you sit turns an abstract effort into a measurable one, and your own previous results become the opponent. For a lot of people that is the version that lasts, because your last split is the most perfectly matched competitor you will ever face.


Live racing sharpens it further, because a real person pulling away from you is harder to ignore than a number in a table. But the benchmark version works on its own too. Aviron member Justin Jackson marked a session simply with "Today I hit my goal of rowing 5,000 consecutive meters," which is competition with nobody but the version of himself who could not do that yet.


One honest caveat. Leaderboards motivate when the field is beatable. A global ranking topped by athletes you will never match is not a competition, it is a scoreboard you happen to appear on. What matters is matched competition, and the option to race yourself. We made the broader case in[the importance of fitness leaderboards](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/Importance-of-fitness-leaderboards) .


## Gamified Fitness Is Not Only for Gamers


It would be easy to read all of this as a niche product for people who own a console. It is not, and the member quoted above is the clearest evidence: what they identify as the reason it works is being *competitive* , not being a gamer.


**You do not need to play video games to enjoy game-based workouts.** If you are motivated by competition, by progress you can see, or by beating your own personal best, the mechanics are already aimed at you. Anyone who has ever checked a race result, tracked a lift, or wanted to know their split time is responding to exactly the same thing.


In practice the appeal spreads across several groups that do not look alike:


- **Gamers** , who recognize the loops immediately. As Aviron member Kelsey Kerling, who grew up on Sega, PlayStation and N64, put it: "I CANNOT TELL YOU HOW ADDICTING IT IS!"
- **Current and former athletes** , who are used to training against a number. Stephan Richmond, a former NFL player, noted that "the level of variety within the programing is far beyond any other brand."
- **Anyone chasing a measurable goal** , whether that is a 2,000m split, a streak, or simply more sessions this month than last.
- **People who find cardio unbearably dull** , which is a larger group than any of the above and the one most likely to have a machine gathering dust.


## Different Ways to Stay Motivated


Games are the sharpest expression of this, but they are not the whole of it, and a platform built only on games would fail for the same reason a platform built only on classes does. Some days you do not want the thing you wanted last week.


Aviron World, which runs on every Aviron machine, is built as a set of different ways in rather than one:


- **Workout games** , where your rowing, riding or running controls what happens on screen.
- **Leaderboards and live competition** , including head-to-head races against other members.
- **Guided workouts and structured programs** , for when you would rather be told what to do than decide.
- **Scenic destinations** , for a session with no scoreboard at all.
- **On-demand classes** , if a coach is what gets you moving.
- **Interval formats** such as Pros vs Joes and Power Play, which add structure without adding a narrative.
- **Streaming apps** , for the nights when the honest answer is that you just want to watch something.


That adds up to more than 1,000 programs, and the point of listing them is not the number. It is that you are not committing to one type of workout forever when you buy the machine.


## Why Variety Matters for Consistency


Go back to the original problem. Cardio gets abandoned because it becomes repetitive, so anything that solves it has to keep working after the novelty wears off.


A single mechanic, however good, eventually becomes the thing you are bored of. Games included. The protection against that is having somewhere else to go on a given evening: competition when you feel sharp, a scenic route when you are tired, a class when you cannot face choosing, a show when you want the session to pass unnoticed.


Aviron member Jorge Zuniga described the pattern well: "I have never been the kind of person to stick to working out well. I fall off the horse constantly. But with Aviron on days I just want to YouTube binge, I do that while rowing. When I have the energy for high intensity there's workouts for that. If I'm feeling competitive, I can do that."


That is what long-term consistency actually looks like. Not the same session repeated with discipline, but a machine you can meet where you are on the day. It is why **92% of Aviron members are still working out a year later** , and we dug further into the mechanism in[the science of workout variety](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/science-of-workout-variety) .


## Which Cardio Machine Is Best for Gamers?


There is no single answer, and anyone who gives you one is selling. The right machine is the one whose movement you will happily repeat several times a week, because that is the variable that decides everything else.


What is worth understanding is that there is no handset. The way you move the machine is the way you play, so each one plays differently in practice.


Pull, pedal or pick up the pace. That is the whole control scheme.


On a rower you pull harder or quicken the stroke, and the game reads both. The screenshot at the top of this article shows exactly that: the game is asking for 26 to 27 strokes a minute, held for 9 seconds, in exchange for bonus points. On a bike you pedal faster or add resistance, and a climb on screen becomes a climb in your legs. On a treadmill you lift the pace or raise the incline, and the terrain rises with you.


- **Running or walking?** A treadmill. Pace is a steady input rather than a twitchy one, which suits endurance formats and being chased better than anything needing quick reactions.
- **Full-body cardio?** The Strong Series Rower. Each stroke is a discrete, powerful input with a magnitude attached, which maps onto game mechanics precisely, and it works most of your body while it does.
- **Cycling?** The Fit Bike S. Cadence and resistance give you two smooth axes you can hold for an hour, which is why it suits racing and long sessions.


The thing that matters more than the choice is that it is not really a choice about content. Aviron World runs across the rowers, bikes and treadmills, so the games, races, routes and classes come with whichever machine fits your body and your room.

## What to Look For in an Interactive Cardio Machine


Whatever brand you end up considering, these are the questions worth asking. Several of them are uncomfortable for manufacturers, which is why they are useful.


What to check Why it matters


Does your effort drive the game? The line between interactive and a screen playing nearby.


Workout variety One format gets stale. Look for genuinely different modes, not reskins.


Competitive features Live racing and matched leaderboards, not just a global ranking.


Progression Can you see improvement over months, and does the content scale with you?


Screen experience Size, responsiveness, and whether it pivots for off-machine use.


Equipment quality Motor, frame, capacity and warranty. Software cannot rescue bad hardware.


Life without a subscription Some machines lose almost everything. Ask before you buy, not after.


Will you use it three times a week? The only question that actually predicts the outcome.


That last row is not a throwaway. Every other specification is a proxy for it.


## The Best Cardio Machine Is One You Actually Want to Use


The best cardio machine is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that gives you a reason to come back tomorrow.


For people motivated by games, competition and measurable progress, gamified fitness can turn cardio from something you have to do into something you actually want to do. That shift is worth more over a year than any specification on the box, because a machine used four times a week beats a better machine used twice a month, every time.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is gamified fitness?


Gamified fitness applies game mechanics such as points, scores, challenges, achievements, competition and leaderboards to exercise. Instead of a workout measured only in time, distance or calories, the session has a goal inside it. In the strongest versions your physical effort is the control input, so the game responds directly to how hard you work.


### Are workout games effective?


For consistency, yes, and consistency is what determines results. The physical work is the same as a conventional session, so the fitness benefit is the same. What changes is adherence, because directing your attention away from fatigue makes a given effort feel easier, and how a workout feels while you are doing it predicts whether you repeat it.


### Can gaming make exercise more motivating?


It can, particularly for people who respond to competition or visible progress. A score to beat, a challenge to complete or a player to catch replaces the clock as the thing you are focused on. Leaderboards add accountability that does not depend on willpower, since you are trying not to lose a position rather than talking yourself into a session.


### What is the best exercise equipment for gamers?


It depends on the movement you enjoy rather than the games themselves. A rower gives the most expressive input and a full-body workout, a bike suits long sessions and racing, and a treadmill fits endurance formats if running is already part of your week. On Aviron the interactive content is the same across all three, so the machine choice comes down to your body and your space.


### What should I look for in an interactive cardio machine?


Check whether your effort actually drives the content, how varied the library is, whether competition is live or only a ranking, how progress is tracked, the screen size and responsiveness, the underlying hardware quality and warranty, and what the machine still does without a subscription. Above all, be honest about whether you will use it several times a week.


### Do you have to be a gamer to enjoy gamified fitness?


No. You do not need to own a console or play video games at all. The mechanics appeal to anyone motivated by competition, progress or beating a personal best, which includes current and former athletes, people training toward a measurable goal, and anyone who simply finds ordinary cardio too monotonous to sustain.
